title: Microsoft dissects the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply-chain compromise
subtitle: A malicious release of a widely-used LLM proxy ran credential-stealing code whenever Python started — no import required — and reached PyPI and official Docker images for about two hours before takedown.
author: AESOP AI Engine
body: Microsoft Threat Intelligence published a detailed post-mortem on October 23 of the LiteLLM 1.107.0 supply-chain attack that briefly hit PyPI and the project's official Docker images on October 21. The malicious release stayed online for roughly two hours before maintainers pulled it, but in that window a credential stealer and a second-stage Unix loader were shipped to anyone who ran pip install for that version — or started Python inside an affected environment at all. Microsoft's write-up shows that LiteLLM did not need to be imported for the payload to run: the package planted three startup files (cook.pth, cook.py, and sitecustomize.py) outside its own directory, and Python's site-initialization executed them whenever the interpreter launched.

The collector swept developer and AI-assistant configs, cloud and Kubernetes credentials, SSH keys, environment variables, browser data, and selected LiteLLM proxy database records; it encrypted the haul with AES-256 and RSA and uploaded it to a LiteLLM-branded lookalike domain. According to LiteLLM's maintainers, the attackers used stolen GitHub CLI OAuth tokens from three engineers to redirect the release workflow to an attacker-controlled source repository and get the release approved by a second compromised account. Microsoft says it has not independently confirmed how the attacker first obtained those tokens.

The incident matters because LiteLLM sits on the exact seam where AI applications meet cloud infrastructure. Datadog puts weekly downloads at roughly 23 million; the proxy brokers calls to more than a hundred model providers and is deployed inside CI pipelines, agent frameworks, and production inference stacks. Credentials harvested from those environments are the keys to model APIs, cloud accounts, and in some cases the LiteLLM proxy database itself. Microsoft's recommended remediation is unusually blunt: 'removing the package or a release tag is not sufficient recovery' — rebuild from verified artifacts, rotate every credential the affected machines could reach, and audit outbound traffic. The safe pinned version is 1.106.2.

A note for learners: this is a textbook case of why modern AI security is largely software supply-chain security. The attack did not target a model, a prompt, or a vector store — it targeted a developer tool everyone trusts. The useful skills are mundane and transferable: pin dependency versions, scope tokens narrowly, run installs in isolated environments, and know what your interpreter runs on startup. The glamor is in the model layer; the breaches live one layer down.
